Political will and capacity to implement already existing obligations and commitments should be strengthened. Coherence, harmonization, and interoperability between the different instruments should be promoted. That is also true for the tools at the disposal of the Security Council for curbing conflict financing. One such example is targeted sanctions, and it is important to ensure that this tool can be fully utilized when appropriate and necessary, and that these measures are effectively enforced. All of this requires multi-stakeholder and international cooperation, as well as readiness to adapt to changing realities. That brings me to my second point. It is important that governance frameworks remain fit for purpose. Case in point is the Kimberley Process. Since its launch in 2003, it has been— it has played an important role in curbing the trade of conflict diamonds. However, its narrow conflict diamond definition limits ability to address the full spectrum of challenges, including diamonds associated with human rights abuses or different kinds of armed conflict. It has not been able, for instance, to address how Russia's diamonds are funding its war of aggression against Ukraine. The modern gold rush also deserves a closer examination. Not uniquely, but discrepancies in production and trade statistics in certain countries raise concerns that gold is being sourced through illicit supply chains, including from conflict-affected areas. I already mentioned Sudan, where an insatiable external demand for gold generates revenue for both parties to the conflict that have caused unspeakable suffering. Being notoriously hard to trace, gold trade is also increasingly associated with organized crime networks, which are seeking to gain control over extraction sites, trade routes, and refining infrastructure. It exposes vulnerable communities to violence and exploitation. Unchecked, these trends can be detrimental to stability. Third, we appreciate that the presidency has also highlighted the impact of climate change for this discussion. Indeed, climate change is increasing pressure on natural resources, exacerbating already existing vulnerabilities in conflict-affected settings. For instance, competition over scarce water resources or pasture during transhumance creates intercommunal tensions that can erupt in violence. And it is important to build resilience of affected communities, including through climate-sensitive mediation that accounts for competition for natural resources. The UN system has the insight and experience to accompany these communities on this journey. In conclusion, Madam President, the overarching principle is clear: natural resources should contribute to peace and development, not perpetuate violence and conflict. And the Security Council can play a significant part in upholding it and ensuring accountability when it is betrayed. And Latvia will continue to advocate for good governance of natural resources as a foundation for peace, security, and prosperity.

Thank you.
I thank the representative of Latvia, and I now give the floor to the representative of Panama.

Gracias.

Thank you, Madam President. Your Excellencies, we convey our greetings to the ministers, the high authorities, and the representatives of delegations who honor us with their participation in this important high-level debate. We value the interesting briefings that they— that the Secretary-General, Antonio Guterres, provided, as well as Ms. Ngozi Nkong'o-Iweala, the Director-General of the World Trade Organization. We'd like to thank the Democratic Republic of the Congo, particularly Her Excellency Thérèse Kayekwamba Wagner, for convening us to a discussion which doesn't only belong to the present but rather to the very future of the international order. Because today we are not only gathered to discuss natural resources. We are meeting to ponder a more far-reaching question: will the world be capable of governing what it needs for its own survival? For a long time, we regarded natural resources as an economic matter. But the 21st century is forcing us to understand them differently. Today, these resources are synonymous with power, the energy transition, technology, social stability, and in too many places, they also mark the precise point where violence starts. Madam President, For this reason, this debate is not a comfortable one. The current reality shows us that the wealth of some territories continues to be exploited by illicit actors, perpetuating insecurity and depriving their peoples of these resources. That they ought to generate and further entrenching poverty. Our country knows from its own history that managing a strategic asset demands much more than infrastructure. It demands a statewide vision. The Panama Canal has taught us that there are assets whose importance extends beyond national borders, but it has also taught us that true sovereignty doesn't mean simply controlling a resource. Rather, it means governing it responsibly and efficiently with a long-term perspective. In our case, one of these essential resources is water. Our recent experience of drought reminded us of a simple but powerful truth: when nature is under strain, So too is the economy, logistics, food security, global trade, and international trust. Excellencies, the world is entering into a new era of competition over essential resources. The energy transition requires critical minerals, and technology depends on them. It's a Artificial intelligence needs energy, water, and metals. Modern economies need safe supply chains, secure supply chains. States are seeking to reduce their strategic dependencies. Businesses are seeking access, and markets are seeking to move quickly. But peace needs something more than that. It needs rules. Because when global demand outpaces governance, the resulting vacuum is filled by corruption, coercion, and interests that thrive wherever the state is weak. This Council was created to address threats to peace, but the threats of our time don't always come wearing uniform, bearing a flag, or a declaration of war. Sometimes they are lurking along a smuggling route or behind a mine controlled by armed actors and criminal networks. If we want to avoid conflict, we have to act to prevent it. We have to follow the money before it is used to buy the weapons that fuel conflicts. We need to trace illicitly extracted minerals before they are concealed in a legitimate supply chain, and we need to strengthen institutions before a state's absence is exploited by violent actors. Our country believes that the Security Council should act more consistently across 4 areas. First, prevention. Natural resource governance should be part of the Council's early risk analysis. When a strategic resource becomes trapped in illicit economies, this is no secondary matter. It is a warning sign. Traceability. Responsibility should extend along the entire supply chain. The world needs to know where the minerals that it's using comes from, under which conditions they were extracted, and who has benefited from them. Shared responsibility. No producing country alone can bear the burden of guaranteeing legality. Natural resource governance requires commitments between producers, transit countries, financial centers, companies, and consumers alike. Legitimate governance and accountability. Natural resources alone don't fuel conflicts. They do so when the systems exist that make it possible to hide beneficiaries, evade controls, and transform illicit wealth into political or military power. Panama believes in a governance that doesn't divide the world between those who extract resources and those who profit from them, between those who bear the ambient— the environmental cost and those who reap the technological benefit. We believe in a form of governance based on sovereignty, legality, transparency, transparency, environmental responsibility, and international shared responsibility. Because the defining question of our time isn't simply who possesses the resources. It is how the decisions are taken, how the benefits are distributed, and how the rights of present and future generations are protected. Madam President, history has shown that natural resources Minerals can finance wars, but they can also finance peace. They can sustain criminal economies, or they can strengthen the rule of law. They can become a driver of conflict if they are governed with greed, but they can also become a driver of stability and development if they are governed responsibly. And this is Panama's appeal today. That the Security Council view natural resources not as a peripheral issue, but rather as one of the major governance challenges of the 21st century. It's not about holding up development. It's about asking ourselves what type of development deserves to be called progress. It's not about choosing between the economy or peace. It's about understanding that without peace, no economy is viable, and without an economy, no peace is sustainable. Panama stands ready to work with all members of the Council, with producing states, with regional organizations, the private sector, and with civil society to advance towards this aim. Because in the end, the question is not whether the world needs natural resources. The question is whether we will have the vision, determination, and leadership to govern responsibly that which our common future depends on. Thank you very much.
I thank the representative of Panama, and I now give the floor to the representative of China.

Madam President, I welcome Her Excellency Minister of Foreign Affairs Cao Yuanbao to chair today's meeting and thank Secretary-General Guterres, Thank you, Mr. President, and Director-General Evila for their briefings. Natural resources are precious gifts from the Earth to mankind, the material foundation for human survival and continuous economic and social development. However, conflicts in some regions demonstrate that resources abundance does not automatically lead to development and prosperity, and poor governance can induce and fuel violence and disputes. The international community should join hands to strengthen the governance of natural resources, maintain the stability of global resource supply chain, and contribute to international peace and development. I would like to make 3 points. First, peace and stability are the solid guarantee for the governance of natural resources. Whether it's oil and gas pipelines or mines and forests, without a peaceful and stable environment, natural resources cannot be used to benefit the people. The international community should uphold a common, comprehensive, cooperative, and sustainable security concept, adhere to the peaceful resolution of disputes, urge the parties involved in conflicts to cease military confrontation, support regional countries and organizations in strengthening cooperation, jointly combat the illegal exploitation and smuggling of natural resources, enhance supply chain transparency and traceability, and cut off the reach of armed conflicts to natural resources at its source. At the same time, the causes of armed conflicts are complex and diverse, involving a range of political, social, and economic factors. Natural resources should not be simply regarded as the root cause of conflicts. Still less should normal economic trade and industrial cooperation be subjected to sweeping securitization, politicization, or instrumentalization. Second, fairness and justice are essential prerequisites for cooperation on natural International law grants all countries absolute sovereignty over their resources, a principle that cannot be challenged. Certain countries should cease using pressure, sanctions, and military coercion to seize resources from other countries and must not revert to colonial domination and plunder. Developing countries have the right to fully utilize their natural resources endowments to achieve economic and social development. China supports building an open, inclusive, fair, reasonable, cooperative, win-win, green, and clean critical mineral governance system. Using the pretext of so-called de-risking or safeguarding national security to pursue blocked confrontation and form exclusive small circles will only disrupt market order and undermine the common interest of all countries. Third, sustainable development is the ultimate goal of natural resource development. Past experience has repeatedly shown that the persistence of illegal exploitation of natural resources is rooted in deeper problems such as poverty, unemployment, and underdevelopment. To break the vicious circle in which resources and conflicts coexist, it is essential to support the countries concerned in achieving sustainable development on their own. The international community, especially developed countries, has the responsibility to fulfill its aid commitments. Support resource-rich countries, particularly developing countries, to continuously improve their resource governance system and to increase the added value and income of resource products through technology transfer, capacity building, talent training, and industrial upgrading, thereby eliminating poverty, increasing employment, truly benefiting local communities, and building a more solid foundation for peace. Madam President, as a major producer, consumer, and trader of natural resources, China has been consistently advocating and promoting governance and cooperation on natural resources. Last year, at the G20 Summit, China put forward the International Economic and Trade Cooperation Initiative on Green Mining and Minerals to promote the establishment of a new type of partnership on mineral resource that's open, win-win, fair, and reasonable. China stands ready to work with the international community to deepen mutually beneficial cooperation on natural resources, better assist relevant countries in transforming their resource endowments into drivers of development, and help them embark on a path of long-term stability, development, and prosperity. I thank you.
I thank the representative of China, and I now give the floor to the representative of Bahrain.

Your Excellencies, at the outset, I am pleased to welcome Her Excellency Ms. Thérèse Kayakomba Wagner, Minister of Foreign Affairs, International Cooperation, and Francophonie in the friendly Democratic Republic of the Congo, and we thank her for presiding over today's session. I also wish to express my sincere appreciation to His Excellency the Secretary-General and to Dr. Okonjo, Director-General of the WTO, for their valuable briefings. We also welcome the participation of the Secretary-General of the GCC, Mr. Badawi, and all those taking part in today's session. Madam President, we meet today to discuss the pivotal role of natural resources in supporting peace and security. These resources encompass multiple sectors, including critical minerals, for which demand is expected to nearly triple by 2030. They also include energy, water, and agricultural resources. Each of these sectors faces challenges related to their effective management and sustainability, as they are fundamental drivers of stability and development. Meanwhile, poor management or competition over these resources increase tensions and conflicts. Therefore, strengthening governance, transparency, and international cooperation in the management of natural resources constitutes a fundamental pillar to ensure their role in promoting peace, development, and shared prosperity. In this regard, I would like to address 3 main points. First, sustainable governance of natural resources is a fundamental pillar for safeguarding international peace and security. International experience confirms that natural resources are not only a source of growth but may also become a factor of instability in the absence of sound governance and in the presence of illicit exploitation, particularly in the mining sector, where revenues may be used to sustain conflicts. Accordingly, reducing the risks of resource-related conflicts requires strengthening governance before crises escalate. This can be achieved through the development of early warning mechanisms to monitor tensions linked to natural resources, and by supporting mediation and peacebuilding efforts, enhancing transparency and the rule of law. Such measures help ensure that natural resources serve as a foundation for stability and sustainable development rather than a cause of conflict. Second, conflicts related to natural resources can have severe humanitarian consequences. They disrupt agricultural activities, damage the environment and livelihoods, thereby threatening food security and undermining the stability of communities. Conflicts are among the main drivers of hunger worldwide. According to data from the World Food Programme, 70% of those facing acute food insecurity live in conflict-affected countries. While 12 of the world's 13 hunger hotspots are located in conflict-affected regions. These facts underscore the urgent need to strengthen responsible governance of natural resources and address the root causes of conflict, as this is the foundation for peacebuilding and humanitarian response. Third, addressing resource-related conflicts require international cooperation. Natural resources are linked to global supply chains, particularly amid increasing tensions that may affect the security of vital transit routes associated with transporting these resources, such as the Strait of Hormuz. Therefore, there is a need to strengthen traceability and transparency systems to promote responsible sourcing and implement due diligence to curb the flow of conflict-linked resources into international markets. The Kingdom also underscores the importance of cooperation among all countries involved in natural resource supply chains alongside support for capacity building. And technical assistance to enhance natural resource management. This would help ensure that producing countries and local communities benefit fairly and sustainably from the revenues generated by their natural resources. The Kingdom further emphasizes the important role of the UN system and regional organizations in developing common governance frameworks in capacity building and exchanging expertise. Madam President, today's debate on natural resources cannot be dissociated from the security of international waterways that ensure these resources reach their intended beneficiaries around the world. In this context, my delegation views with deep concern the continuing threats and repeated attempts by Iran to close or obstruct navigation through the Strait of Hormuz. This strait is not merely a regional waterway. It is a vital artery for the global economy through which a substantial portion of international energy resources flows. Any disruption of navigation through the strait constitutes not only a violation of the freedom of international navigation, but also amounts to using natural resources as a tool of political pressure. Accordingly, and in implementation of Security Council Resolution 2817, the Kingdom of Bahrain renews its call on the international community and this esteemed Council to adopt firm positions to safeguard the freedom of international navigation and protect vital waterways from any threats. This would ensure the secure and safe flow of natural resources and would serve the growth and prosperity of all peoples of the world. In conclusion, Madam President, the Kingdom reaffirms that natural resources should be a means of achieving peace and development, not a source of conflict and instability. This requires strengthening governance and transparency, Building capacities and enhancing international cooperation to ensure the responsible, sustainable development of natural resources in a manner that benefits all countries and communities. Thank you, President.

Madam President, I'd like to begin by thanking you for your presidency of our work today as. Minister of Foreign Affairs of the DRC. So we thank the Congolese Presidency for choosing to further the Council's consideration of this matter. Thank you, Madam President, I'll insist on 2 points. Firstly, the exploitation and illicit trafficking of natural resources are an aggravating factor in many crises on the Council's agenda. In the Democratic Republic of the Congo, in the Central African Republic, in Sudan, in Colombia, or in Myanmar, the appropriation of natural resources sparks conflicts whose toll is borne by civilians. In the east of the DRC, the M23 controls between 15 and 30% of global coltan production at the Rubaya site, thus funding its illegal administration in full violation of Congolese sovereignty and territorial integrity. In Sudan, gold trafficking fuels the war economy, which only serves to prolong a conflict that has caused one of the worst humanitarian crises in the world. Elsewhere on the African continent, these resources are being plundered by local or international actors who sometimes use private military companies to manage the pillaging on behalf of external powers. Secondly, in addressing this scourge, the Council must harness the tools available to it and ensure the strict implementation of existing multilateral mechanisms. This means making full use of Council's panels of experts and sanctions regimes who play a precious role in documenting the facts and disrupting the link between pillaging of natural resources and funding the parties to the conflict. Last week, This Council adopted sanctions against 8 individuals and entities related to armed groups destabilizing the east of the DRC, including the M23, the FDLR, and the ADF terrorist group. As we have repeatedly stressed, we must work so that the sanctions regime relating to Sudan is brought more into line with the reality of the current conflict. This also means providing support to existing multilateral mechanisms such as the Kimberley Process the OECD mechanisms or the International Conference for the Great Lakes Region, as well as the Extractive Industries Transparency Initiative. Finally, this involves ensuring greater accountability on the part of the private sector. France is fully committed in this area, be it through the presidency of the G7 or within the European Union. Madam President, to conclude, the sovereignty of every state over its natural resources is a fundamental issue. These resources should be harnessed for sustainable and equitable development of people's— of countries' populations. France supports the objective expressed by the DRC to work to improve the effectiveness and coherence of international initiatives to ensure the proper use of these resources. Looking to the future, we stand fully ready to contribute to the Council's work to that end. Thank you very much.

Madam President, distinguished members of the Security Council, good afternoon. I'd like to begin by thanking the Democratic Republic of the Congo for convening this debate on a matter which goes beyond the mere management of natural resources and sits at the crux of peace, security, and geopolitics in the 21st century. The energy transition and the technological revolution have conferred unprecedented geostrategic value on critical minerals and rare earths. Their growing global demand has created opportunities for the countries that possess them, but it has also heightened the risks of illicit exploitation and the spread of illegal economies. When that happens, mineral wealth ceases to be a driver of development and becomes a source of violence and instability. The responsible governance of these strategic resources is the first line of defense against against their illicit appropriation by criminal organizations or armed groups. At the same time, it calls for a paradigm shift in international economic relations. Developing countries cannot continue to be seen through the outdated lens of being mere suppliers of raw materials bearing the environmental and social costs of extraction while the added value and technological development remain in the industrialized centers. Cementing a lasting peace means linking the exploitation of critical minerals with technology transfer processes, with the development of local capacities and integration into continental-wide value chains. Solely strengthening— solely by strengthening the sovereign prerogatives of states will we be able to build resilient economies and curb the incentives that fuel criminal structures. Madam President, beyond its devastating environmental impact, illegal mining has become one of the main sources of funds for transnational organized crime. Combating this scourge means acting at every link of the supply chain, illicit extraction is just the beginning of a criminal network which encompasses smuggling, money laundering, corruption, and the international marketing of minerals of dubious origin. It's imperative for this Council to promote binding mechanisms for traceability, certification of origin, and corporate due diligence in destination markets. The advanced industries of the 21st century cannot sustain their supply chains with the same minerals that fund violence. The experience of the Democratic Republic of the Congo shows how illicit exploitation of minerals can undermine peace efforts and can prolong conflicts for decades. Latin American experience— indeed, our continent holds extraordinary geological wealth confirms that illegal economies weaken democratic institutions, erode governability, and allow criminal organizations to control territories and communities. In our region, these dynamics are intertwined with drug trafficking, weapons trafficking, and trafficking in persons, going so far as to fund armed groups that corrode the social fabric of our countries. Today, illicit gold rivals drugs trafficking for profitability, taking advantage of porous borders and a lack of regulation of modern financial tools such as cryptocurrency. This explains the existential struggle that the national government, together with its people, is waging against transnational organized crime. For Ecuador, addressing this challenge is is the main statewide security priority. For this reason, we reaffirm our support for regional cooperation instruments such as the Andean Community's Resolute Action Plan, the Santiago Regional Commitment, and the Shield of the Americas. No state can prevail in isolation. The response must be coordinated, strategic, and multidisciplinary. As the President of Ecuador, Daniel Noboa, has stressed, this is a global challenge demanding an equally global response. The total offensive phase against organized crime, drugs trafficking, and illegal mining began in June. The President stressed that international cooperation will strengthen Ecuador that is no longer battling transnational mafias alone. This initiative is part of a comprehensive national security plan. This is a public policy to dismantle criminal structures that use illegal mining as their main mechanism for funding and money laundering. Since the start of this year alone, more than 1,000 illegal mine shafts have been destroyed nationwide. Madam President, technological innovation and the green transition cannot be built on minerals tainted by violence or economic exclusion of supplier countries. I appeal to this Security Council to incorporate geostrategic governance of natural resources and the fight against their illicit exploitation within their mandates and conflict prevention strategies. The true foundation of international peace and security lies in transforming mineral wealth into an instrument for equity, legality, and development for all nations. Thank you very much.
I thank His Excellency Mr. Koury Per-Santis for that statement, and I now give the floor to His Excellency Mr. Tete Antonio, Minister for External Relations of Angola.

Thank you, Madam President. Excellencies, Madame Thérèse Kayikwamba Wagner, Minister of State and Minister of Foreign Affairs and International Cooperation for the Francophonie of Congolese in the Diaspora of the Democratic Republic of the Congo. We wish to begin by extending our congratulations to the DRC in light of its— under the leadership of its President for this outstanding Security Council presidency. We'd also like to pay tribute to the President— the presence this morning of the Secretary General, and we thank him for his briefing. And I convey my greetings to my dear sister, Ngozi Okonjo-Iweala, the Director-General of the WTO. We thank her for a very helpful briefing.

Resources are often considered a blessing, but they can also become a curse only depending on certain factors like the way they are governed. Where governance is transparent, accountable, and effective, natural resources to drive, certainly, economic growth, strengthen institutions, and improve livelihoods. Where governance is challenged, they can fuel conflict, finance armed groups, undermine state authority, and deprive populations of the benefits of their own wealth. The challenge before us today is therefore not the availability of natural resources, but the quality of the governance also matters. Angola wishes to highlight therefore 3 priorities. The first one is strengthen governance frameworks. Member states should reinforce legal, regulatory, and institutional frameworks governing access to extraction and the trade in natural resources in full respect of the sovereignty of the countries of origin. Illegal exploitation must be addressed through effective enforcement, anti-corruption measures, and action against illicit financial flows. Existing international and regional mechanisms, including the Kimberley Process, to which the Republic of Angola contributed by— based on its own experience of a long conflict conflict and the so-called blood diamonds then, the OECD due diligence guidance, the regional certification mechanism of the International Conference of the Great Lakes Region, and the Extractive Industries Transparency Initiative provide valuable foundations for that. Our collective priority should therefore be strengthen their implementation, traceability, forward global supply chains, and harness emerging technologies to enhance transparency and accountability. Second priority is to deepen international cooperation. Illicit exploitation and trafficking of natural resources are transnational challenges that require coordinated responses. Greater cooperation among member states regional organizations, international financial institutions, the private sector, and civil society is essential to strengthen information sharing, enhance customs and law enforcement cooperation, and disrupt criminal networks operating across borders while fully respecting national ownership and the permanent sovereignty of states. over their natural resources. The third priority is to place natural resource governance at the center of conflict prevention, as well as already mentioned by the Minister of Foreign Affairs of the Democratic Republic of Congo. In the Eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo and over conflict-affected regions of Africa. The illegal exploitation of natural resources continues to finance armed groups, sustain violence, and undermine peaceful efforts. Breaking this cycle requires stronger governance, greater domestic value addition, environmental sustainability, meaningful participation of local communities, and sustained investment in national institutions and capacities. Madam President, the Security Council has long recognized the link between the illicit exploitation of natural resources and armed conflict. The priority now is implementation. Natural resource governance should be systematically integrated into conflict prevention, peacebuilding, sanction, implementation, and post-conflict We look forward to learning more about this very valuable initiative. Angola remains convinced that natural resources must become an engine of sustainable development rather than drivers of instability. Achieving the objective requires— this objective requires accountable governance, resilient institutions, responsible partnerships, leadership and sustainable political commitment. Processing locally the critical minerals is one of the drivers of this common effort for economic diversification as well as economic integration for our continent. I'm talking about Africa, including the announcement of the role Of the integration for the infrastructures we have put in place, like the Lobito Corridors, which is a tool of cooperation between Angola, the DRC, and Zambia, and the rest of the African continent. I thank you, Chairperson.

Excellencies, Ms. Thérèse Kayekwambo Wagner, President of the Security Council and Minister of the DRC, dear sister. The excellent briefing from the Secretary-General of the United Nations and the one from my sister Distinguished members of the Council, Excellencies, ladies and gentlemen, the Republic of the Congo welcomes the convening of this important meeting of the United Nations Security Council devoted to the theme Natural Resource Governance: The Foundation of Peace, Security, and Prosperity. Who better than the Democratic Republic of the Congo, which holds the presidency of the Security Council this month, to bring this essential debate to the heart of the institution, our institution that embodies multilateralism, peace, justice, and respect for international law? His Excellency Mr. Denis Sassou Nguesso, President of the Republic of the Congo, whom I have the honor of representing before this distinguished assembly, places peace, Pan-Africanism, the defense of multilateralism, and sustainable management of natural resources at the heart of his political and diplomatic action. His vision rests on a fundamental conviction, namely the primacy of the United Nations Charter and specifically lasting peace, which requires responsible transparent, and equitable governance of natural resources so that their sustainable management can serve as a driver of development, stability, and security. This reality is particularly evident in the Congo Basin and the Great Lakes region, where natural resources are at the heart of development challenges, but at times they are also the cause of tensions and conflict. Globally, nearly 40% of internal conflicts over the past few decades have been linked, whether directly or indirectly, to the issue of natural resources. We therefore welcome the initiative of the Democratic Republic of the Congo. It follows in the tradition of great voices such as that of Ms. Wangari Maathai, Nobel Peace Prize laureate and Goodwill Ambassador for the Congo Basin Forests, who reminded us of the inseparable link between the environment, sustainable development and peace, notably when she declared that investing in the protection and conservation of the environment is an investment in peace.

End of quote.

The Congo Basin, the world's second-largest tropical forest, is a major ecological legacy for humanity. Its preservation is a global challenge that requires collective mobilization. In this light, 2 priorities deserve the attention of the international community. First, strengthening innovative financing mechanism as well as regional cooperation, in particular through the Blue Fund for the Congo Basin, so that climate financing becomes a concrete instrument for peace and development. Second, Support permanent platforms for dialogue and mediation, such as that of the Economic Community of Central African States, ECOWAS, as well as those of the International Conference of the Great Lakes Region, in order to prevent disputes linked to natural resources before they turn into crises. Finally, we call for the ambitious implementation of international initiatives for afforestation, reforestation, and ecosystem restoration. which help ease pressure on natural resources and prevent conflict. This, uh, an example of this is the initiative championed by His Excellency Mr. Denis Sassou-Nguesso, President of the Republic of the Congo, on the United Nations Decade on Afforestation and Reforestation for Sustainable Forest Management 2027-2036, which was adopted here at the UN on April 16th through Resolution A/Res. 79/283.

Thank you.

Excellencies, ladies and gentlemen, by way of conclusion, the Republic of the Congo will continue alongside its African and international partners to work for mediation, conflict prevention, and the sustainable management of natural resources. We thank the Democratic Republic of the Congo, and in particular its head of state, His Excellency Félix-Antoine Tshisekedi Tshilombo, for this pioneering and valuable initiative to which we fully subscribe. Thank you very much for your kind attention.
I thank His Excellency Mr. Bundafra's statement. I now give the floor to His Excellency Mubitalua Belwa, Executive Secretary of the International Conference on the Great Lakes Region.

President of the Security Council and Minister of Foreign Affairs, International Cooperation, Francophone and Congolese Diaspora, Her Excellency Teresa Kaikwamba Wagner, His Excellency Secretary-General of the United Nations and Director-General also of the World Trade Organization, distinguished members of Security Council, ladies and gentlemen. Allow me from the outset— allow me from the outset to thank the chairperson of the International Conference on the Great Lakes Region, His Excellency President Félix-Antoine Tshisekedi President of the DRC, for ably steering the International Conference on the Great Lakes Region as chairperson. This reminds us that those who have borne the heaviest burdens often offer the clearest vision of peace— that is, the peace that we seek, the peace that we must build. The Great Lakes Region faces a critical choice: whether its rich mineral resources continue to to fuel conflict, or will summon the strength to make it a driver of peace and development? The International Conference on the Great Lakes Region has shown that another path exists. To this effect, the International Conference of the Great Lakes Region Regional Certification Mechanism on Tin, Tantalum, Tungsten, and Gold, the 3 Ts and Gold, promotes traceability, transparency, and accountability in mineral supply chains. With thousands of certificates issued so far, in DRC alone more than 33,000 certificates issued to miners over the past few years, significant progress has been made in ensuring that mineral revenues benefit communities rather than armed groups and The certificates are issued across several member states in the ICGR region. The region's experience demonstrates that credible traceability systems, harmonized standards, and strong political commitment can transform the management of natural resources. To sustain this progress, responsible supply chains must be strengthened, artisanal miners must be supported through formalization and access to finance, Local communities must get a fair share of resource benefits, and natural resource governance should be treated not only as an economic issue but also as a cornerstone of peace and security. After 15 years of regional cooperation in the Great Lakes region, the ICGR has shown that minerals can become pillars of stability rather than sources of conflict. Greater local value addition, environmental sustainability, and stronger international support are now essential to convert natural resource wealth into lasting peace, shared prosperity, and sustainable development. This leads us to one conclusion. As proposed by the President, there must be a gathering around this cause, and importantly, this transformative path must be realistic, gradual and incremental. I thank His Excellency Mr. Loua Belwa for his statement, and I now give the floor to His Excellency Mr. Jassim Mohammed Al-Budaiwi, Secretary-General, Cooperation Council for the Arab States of the Gulf.

Bismillahirrahmanirrahim.

In the name of God, the gracious, the merciful. Your Excellency, Madam Theresa Wagner, the Minister of Foreign Affairs, International Cooperation, and Francophonie of the Democratic Republic of the Congo. Excellencies, members of the Council, ladies and gentlemen, peace and God's blessings be upon you. At the outset, I'd like to extend my sincere congratulations to the Democratic Republic of the Congo on its assumption of the Presidency of the Security Council for the current month of July. I would also like to express my sincere appreciation for the kind invitation to participate in this high-level open debate on natural resource governance as a foundation for peace, security, and prosperity. This topic is of growing importance in light of the significant challenges facing the international community and the imperative of strengthening the nexus between security and sustainable development. Madam President, when natural resources are managed in accordance with the principles of good governance, transparency, the rule of law, and international cooperation, they become a powerful driver of development and prosperity at both the national and international levels. However, when they are used as instruments of war or political coercion, or when the infrastructure associated with them is deliberately targeted, or when their supply routes are disrupted, then they become a source of instability with adverse repercussions for the global economy and international peace and security. Guided by this conviction, conviction, the member states of the Gulf Cooperation Council have made the sound governance of natural resources a fundamental pillar of their national and collective policies. GCC member states possess approximately 30% of the world's proven oil reserves and nearly 20% of global natural gas reserves. They account for around a quarter of global oil production. This has established the GCC member states as a reliable partner in maintaining stability in global energy markets, including during times of crisis and geopolitical uncertainty. In this context, the GCC member states have continued to invest the revenues generated from their natural resources in building more diversified and resilient economies. They've invested in human capital and developed infrastructure and continue to foster innovation and implement ambitious national visions. They have expanded investments in renewable energy and low-carbon hydrogen projects. This all reflects the commitment to striking a balance between energy security and climate action. The governance of natural resources cannot be separated from the security of global supply chains, particularly the protection of critical infrastructure and international maritime routes through which global trade and energy supplies pass. This constitutes— or these constitute essential pillars for the stability of the global economy. Accordingly, any attack on these maritime routes or any disruption of navigation through them threatens not only the interests of exporting countries, but also directly undermines global energy security, international supply chains, and the stability of international markets. Madam President, Since the 28th of February, Iran has continued to launch ballistic missile and drone attacks against the member states of the GCC and other countries without any lawful justification and in a flagrant violation of the principles of international law, the Charter of the United Nations, and the rules of good neighborliness. These attacks continue and they pose a grave danger to the GCC member states and to regional and international peace and security. These attacks disrupt the path of development and stability. They place the global economy at serious risk. From this podium, we renew our call upon the international community, foremost among them the Security Council, to discharge its legal responsibilities by putting an end to these attacks and deterring Iran from continuing its aggressive policies in a manner that preserves international peace and security and safeguards the sovereignty and territorial integrity of states These attacks not only target the countries targeted, but also constitute a pattern of conduct that ultimately harms the Iranian people, who continue to bear the consequences of a regime that squanders the nation's resources on escalation and conflict rather than directing these resources towards development and prosperity and improving the living standards of its citizens while securing their future. This Iranian conduct is unacceptable. It is inconsistent with the Charter of the United Nations. It undermines international efforts aimed at promoting peace, security, and prosperity.
